strengths: Novel and biologically well-motivated core idea: using real gene knockdown experiments (from LINCS) as 'teacher' supervision for contrastive augmentation in GRNs, rather than relying on purely artificial random perturbations as in standard GCL.

Principled theoretical framework: the paper formulates SupGCL within the I-CON KL-divergence contrastive learning framework, proves a clean decomposition (Theorem 1) showing the loss splits into a node-level GCL term (reweighted by supervised augmentation probabilities) plus an augmentation-alignment term, and shows conventional GCL emerges as a temperature limit (Corollary 1), giving the method solid conceptual grounding.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 13 downstream tasks (3 node-level, 2 graph-level) across three cancer types (breast, lung, colorectal), built from real TCGA patient data and LINCS knockdown data, compared against multiple relevant baselines (GAE, GraphCL, GRACE, SGRL) with 10-fold CV or repeated undersampling protocols.

Extensive appendix materials supporting reproducibility: detailed dataset construction (TCGA/LINCS extraction, GO/OncoKB labeling), GRN estimation methodology (Bayesian network with B-spline regression), hyperparameter search details, and compute/time statistics.

Useful supplementary analyses beyond headline numbers: additional metrics (macro-F1, Jaccard), latent space visualization (t-SNE, PCA) revealing GraphCL's representational collapse, and a study of robustness across embedding dimensions, which strengthens confidence in the qualitative claims.
weaknesses: Statistical significance is not rigorously established: many reported gains for SupGCL over the best baseline are well within one standard deviation of overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., Table 2 BP Breast: 0.243±0.052 vs. w/o-pretrain 0.232±0.031; Rel. tasks show similarly small margins), yet the text claims SupGCL 'consistently outperformed' baselines without providing paired statistical tests despite having per-fold results readily available.

The claimed node-level representation benefit is undercut by the paper's own latent space analysis, which finds 'no clear clustering' by BP labels for any method including SupGCL in the t-SNE visualizations; the strongest qualitative separation is observed only at the graph level, suggesting the node-level improvements reported quantitatively may not correspond to biologically interpretable structure.

Coverage limitation of the supervision signal: teacher GRNs are only available for a subset of genes (e.g., 768/975 for breast), so the augmentation set K used for supervised contrastive learning does not span the full gene set; the impact of this partial coverage on the learned representations for genes lacking knockdown data is not analyzed.

Generalization is narrow and explicitly acknowledged as a limitation: teacher GRNs are drawn from the same cancer type/cell line as the target GRNs (MCF7, A549, HT29 only), so it remains unverified whether the biological supervision signal transfers across cancer types or unseen cell lines, limiting the practical significance of the claimed generality.

The method depends on a computationally heavy GRN construction pipeline (Bayesian network estimation via B-spline regression run on a supercomputer, taking up to ~21 hours on hundreds of Fugaku nodes), which raises practical reproducibility/accessibility concerns for typical research groups without HPC access, beyond the GCL training itself.

Related work comparisons are somewhat incomplete: BGRL is discussed conceptually but not included as an experimental baseline, and the connection/contrast to general supervised contrastive learning (e.g., SupCon-style methods outside the graph domain) is not discussed, making it harder to situate the specific contribution relative to the broader supervised contrastive learning literature.

The independence assumption pϕ(i,j,a,b) = p(i,j)pϕ(a,b) used to derive the trivial-solution-avoiding decomposition (Theorem 1) is a modeling simplification whose validity/impact is not empirically examined.

Minor presentation issue: the code/data availability statement is incomplete ('available on' with no link or repository given), which limits verifiability of the reproducibility claims made in the paper.

strengths: The core idea—replacing artificial graph perturbations in GCL with biologically grounded gene-knockdown perturbations from LINCS as supervision for GRN representation learning—is a genuine and well-motivated contribution that addresses a real gap in applying generic GCL to biological networks.

The method is grounded in a clean probabilistic/KL-divergence framework (following the I-CON formulation), and the paper provides a rigorous derivation (Theorem 1) showing that conventional node-level GCL emerges as a special case of SupGCL in the high-temperature limit (Corollary 1), lending theoretical coherence to the proposal.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad: three cancer types (breast, lung, colorectal), five downstream tasks (13 task/cancer combinations), and comparisons against several representative GCL baselines (GAE, GraphCL, GRACE, SGRL), plus extensive appendix material (additional metrics, latent-space PCA/t-SNE visualizations, embedding-dimension ablations, detailed data-processing pipeline).

Reasonable transparency about data construction (TCGA + LINCS), the Bayesian-network GRN estimation procedure, and hyperparameter tuning via Optuna, which aids methodological reproducibility of the pipeline in principle.
weaknesses: Many of the reported improvements are not statistically distinguishable from baselines given the reported standard deviations (e.g., Table 2 Rel.-Breast: SupGCL 0.600±0.057 vs. SGRL 0.580±0.055; Table 3 Hazard-Lung: 0.627±0.051 vs. GAE 0.619±0.062), yet the abstract and contributions claim SupGCL 'achieves better performance than state-of-the-art baselines' and 'consistently outperform[s] conventional approaches across all tasks' without any significance testing (e.g., paired tests across folds) to substantiate this claim.

Results are inconsistent across metrics for the same task: e.g., in Appendix Table 10, GraphCL actually obtains the best macro-F1 for BP classification on Lung (0.584) and ties/exceeds SupGCL on Colorectal CC, which is not reconciled with the main-text claim of consistent superiority based on subset accuracy alone; this selective metric emphasis undermines the soundness of the 'consistently outperforms' narrative.

Absolute performance on several node-level tasks is low (e.g., ~0.23–0.29 subset accuracy for 3–4 class multi-label BP/CC classification), and no naive/majority-class or upper-bound baselines are reported, making it hard to judge whether the learned representations are practically useful beyond marginal numeric gains over an untrained model.

The central assumption—that GRNs derived from cancer cell-line shRNA knockdown experiments (LINCS) are valid 'teacher' signals for patient tumor GRNs (TCGA)—is a strong biological leap (in vitro cell-line perturbation vs. in vivo patient tumor networks) that is not empirically validated or critically discussed; the paper only acknowledges as a limitation that teacher/target cancer types must match, not the more fundamental cross-modality assumption.

The code availability sentence in Section 2 ('Our implementation and all experimental codes are available on') is truncated with no actual link, which is a reproducibility and presentation flaw; additionally, the GRN estimation pipeline relies on a specialized supercomputer (Fugaku) with substantial compute (up to ~21 hours across hundreds of nodes), which severely limits practical reproducibility for most readers.

No comparison is made to any biologically-specialized or GRN-specific representation learning baselines beyond generic GCL methods (e.g., GCLink, which is cited as prior work applying GRACE to GRNs, or domain-specific GRN embedding approaches), leaving the significance of the contribution relative to the closest prior biological-network-adapted methods unclear.

The paper itself concedes in the conclusion that effectiveness was only verified when teacher and target GRNs come from the same cancer type, and no cross-cancer or held-out generalization experiments are provided, limiting the demonstrated scope of the contribution.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing GCL methods use artificial perturbations that are biologically implausible for GRNs, and the paper proposes a principled way to inject real gene-knockdown experimental data (from LINCS) as supervision.

Clean theoretical formulation: the paper casts GCL within the general KL-divergence/I-CON contrastive framework and derives SupGCL as a joint node+augmentation-level objective, proving (Theorem 1 and Corollary 1) that conventional (unsupervised) node-level GCL is recovered as the high-temperature limit of SupGCL. This gives a principled way to interpolate between purely artificial and fully biologically-supervised augmentation.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation: 13 downstream tasks (3 node-level, 2 graph-level) across three cancer types (breast, lung, colorectal), using real patient GRNs (TCGA) and real knockdown-derived teacher GRNs (LINCS), compared against five relevant baselines (GAE, GraphCL, GRACE, SGRL, no-pretrain).

Thorough appendix supporting reproducibility and robustness: detailed dataset construction (Bayesian-network GRN estimation with B-spline nonparametric regression), hyperparameter search protocol via Optuna, additional metrics (Macro-F1, Jaccard), PCA/t-SNE latent space analyses showing GraphCL's representational collapse, and an embedding-dimension sensitivity study.

The consistent (if sometimes small) improvement of SupGCL across nearly all 13 tasks, together with qualitatively cleaner subtype separation in the latent space visualizations, provides converging evidence (not just single-metric superiority) for the method's benefit.
weaknesses: The code availability statement is broken ("Our implementation and all experimental codes are available on" with no link provided), undermining reproducibility despite the otherwise detailed appendix.

No statistical significance testing is performed despite reporting means and standard deviations across folds/seeds; in several tables the gap between SupGCL and the best baseline is well within one standard deviation (e.g., Rel. task, Hazard for lung/breast), and the paper itself concedes SupGCL is not statistically superior in every task, weakening the strength of the "consistently outperforms" claim.

The additional-metric tables in the appendix (Macro-F1, Jaccard) sometimes contradict the main-text accuracy tables — e.g., for BP-Lung, GraphCL attains the best Macro-F1 (0.584) while performing far worse in subset accuracy — suggesting the improvements may partly reflect metric/threshold artifacts (e.g., class imbalance effects) rather than robust representational gains, and this discrepancy is not analyzed or explained.

Method requires patient-matched teacher GRNs built from actual knockdown experiments of the same cancer type/cell line, which is a strong data requirement; the paper's own stated limitation (only tested within same-cancer teacher/target pairs) raises questions about generalizability to genes/cancers lacking such paired perturbation data, and this is not empirically explored (e.g., cross-cancer transfer).

Computational cost of SupGCL is substantially higher than baselines (up to ~21 hours pretraining vs. a few hours for others), which is not discussed as a trade-off against the often marginal performance gains.

The core theoretical contribution (decomposing joint KL divergence into node-conditional and augmentation-marginal terms) is a fairly direct application of the standard chain rule for KL divergence; the technical novelty resides mainly in the domain-specific instantiation (using knockdown data as teacher distributions) rather than in fundamentally new contrastive learning theory.
Graph-level subtype classification is validated only for breast cancer (the only cancer type with subtype labels), limiting the breadth of evidence for this particular downstream task.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core idea: repurposing biologically meaningful knockdown perturbations as supervisory signals for GCL rather than treating structural augmentation as noise to be eliminated, addressing a real gap between augmentation-free GCL trends and the opportunity to use real experimental perturbation data.

Clean theoretical contribution: the paper derives a probabilistic formulation (via KL-divergence decomposition) that shows conventional node-level GCL emerges as a limiting case (Corollary 1) of the proposed supervised augmentation framework, giving the method principled generality rather than being an ad hoc heuristic.

Extensive and carefully constructed empirical evaluation: 13 downstream tasks (3 node-level, 2 graph-level) across 3 real cancer types built from TCGA (patient GRNs) and LINCS (knockdown GRNs), with consistent improvement trends over strong baselines (GAE, GraphCL, GRACE, SGRL).

Very thorough supplementary analysis addressing many natural reviewer concerns: statistical significance testing, alternative metrics (F1, Jaccard), embedding-dimension sensitivity, comparison to augmentation-correction/augmentation-free methods (GCA, AFGRL, SimGRACE), link-prediction evaluation, cross-domain generalization study, robustness to sample size/noise in GRN estimation, and biological enrichment (GO/KEGG) analysis of learned representations, which together substantially strengthen credibility of the contribution.
Honest and specific limitations discussion (failure to generalize across cancer types at fine-tuning stage) rather than vague hedging.
Detailed reproducibility documentation (hyperparameters, computational environment, preprocessing pipeline) in the appendix.
weaknesses: Many of the reported improvements are numerically small relative to standard deviations (e.g., Table 2: SupGCL 0.243±0.052 vs GRACE 0.230±0.051 for BP-Breast), and the formal significance testing (Table 15, Appendix F.4) finds statistically significant differences only against GraphCL and SGRL in a handful of node-level tasks, not against the strongest baselines (GAE, GRACE) in most cases — this undercuts the abstract's claim of 'consistently outperforms' in a strong sense.

The independence assumption used to derive Theorem 1 (that the joint distribution factorizes as p(i,j,a,b)=p(i,j)p(a,b)) is a modeling convenience rather than something empirically or theoretically justified, and its implications for the tightness/validity of the decomposition are not discussed.

There is an unaddressed domain-mismatch concern: teacher GRNs are derived from cancer cell-line knockdown experiments (LINCS) while target graphs are patient-specific GRNs estimated from TCGA; the assumption that cell-line perturbation effects meaningfully transfer as supervisory signal to patient-derived networks is not rigorously validated beyond aggregate downstream performance.

Reproducibility is constrained by a highly specialized and computationally expensive GRN-estimation pipeline (custom Bayesian network software INGOR run on the Fugaku supercomputer with hundreds of nodes and hours to tens of hours), which likely limits independent replication by most academic groups despite detailed documentation.

The paper acknowledges but does not resolve poor cross-cancer-type generalization at the fine-tuning stage, which meaningfully limits the practical significance of the pretrained representations for a general-purpose GRN foundation model.

Presentation is dense in places (heavy notation for the probabilistic formulation), and the large number of appendix analyses, while thorough, could be better synthesized in the main text to make the core empirical takeaways clearer to readers.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely interesting: rather than treating structural perturbations in GCL as noise to be avoided (as in the augmentation-free trend), the paper reframes real biological perturbations (gene knockdown data) as a supervisory signal, which is a sensible and underexplored direction for GRN representation learning.

The probabilistic formulation is reasonably clean: the paper decomposes the supervised loss into a node-level term and an augmentation-level term via a standard KL decomposition, and shows that conventional (unsupervised) node-level GCL is recovered as a limiting case (Corollary 1) as the augmentation temperature grows, which gives some theoretical grounding to the framework.

The empirical evaluation is broad in scope: 13 downstream tasks across three cancer types (breast, lung, colorectal), both node-level (BP/CC/cancer-relation classification) and graph-level (hazard prediction, subtype classification) tasks, built from real TCGA and LINCS data, plus an extensive appendix covering ablations on temperature, embedding dimension, link prediction, cross-domain transfer, robustness to GRN estimation noise, and biological enrichment analysis.
Reproducibility details (hyperparameters, computation times, pseudocode, dataset construction pipeline) are thoroughly documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central claim that SupGCL 'consistently outperforms' baselines is only true in terms of point estimates; the paper's own significance testing (Appendix F.4) shows that after Bonferroni correction, only a handful of comparisons (vs. GraphCL and SGRL on a few node-level tasks) reach significance, while comparisons against GAE and GRACE—arguably the more competitive baselines—are not shown to be statistically significant anywhere. Given the large standard deviations relative to the gaps (e.g., Table 2 BP-Breast: 0.243±0.052 vs 0.230±0.051; Table 3 Hazard-Breast: 0.650±0.059 vs 0.642±0.064), the practical significance of the improvements is questionable.

The 'biological perturbation' used as supervision is itself an approximation: knockdown data come from cancer cell lines (LINCS: MCF7, A549, HT29) while the patient graphs are Bayesian-network estimates from TCGA tumor expression data. The paper does not empirically validate the core assumption that a cell-line knockdown response transfers meaningfully to the same gene's role in a patient-specific estimated network; this cross-domain mismatch (cell line vs. patient, and estimated vs. observed network) is a significant unaddressed gap given that it underlies the entire supervisory signal.

The augmentation operation itself is still just zeroing out node/edge features for the 'knocked-down' gene, essentially the same node/edge-dropping augmentation the introduction criticizes as biologically unfaithful; the novelty is limited to supervising this same crude operation with a teacher embedding, which weakens the framing that this approach fundamentally differs from (and improves upon) the criticized artificial-augmentation paradigm.

A key limitation acknowledged by the authors themselves (fine-tuned models do not transfer across cancer types, Appendix G) substantially limits the claimed generality/significance of a 'general-purpose' representation learning approach, since practical deployment on new cancer types would require re-collecting large knockdown supervision sets per cancer type.

SupGCL incurs substantially higher pretraining cost than baselines (e.g., ~21 hours vs. 3–11 hours for GAE/GraphCL/SGRL on breast cancer, Table 11), which is a real practical cost not sufficiently discussed relative to the modest performance gains.

The theoretical contribution (Theorem 1) is a direct application of the standard KL divergence chain-rule decomposition and does not represent a particularly deep or surprising theoretical insight, despite being marketed as a main contribution.

The downstream label spaces used for evaluation are coarse (3 BP classes, 4 CC classes, 5 subtypes), and the sample sizes for some cancer types (e.g., colorectal, N=288) are small, raising concerns about the statistical reliability of the reported metrics and their generalizability.

The comparison to GCLink, a supervised GNN method purpose-built for GRN inference, is relegated to the appendix and uses a 'modified variant,' making it hard to assess how the proposed method compares to the closest existing line of supervised GRN-based work under fair conditions.

strengths: Well-motivated and genuinely novel idea: rather than treating augmentation-induced structural change as noise to avoid (as in the augmentation-free GCL trend), the paper reframes real biological perturbations (gene knockdown experiments) as a natural, information-rich supervisory signal for GCL on GRNs.

Rigorous theoretical formulation: the paper derives SupGCL from a unified KL-divergence/contrastive-learning framework, proves a clean decomposition (Theorem 1) into node-level and augmentation-level losses, and shows conventional unsupervised GCL emerges as a limiting case (Corollary 1) as τ_a → ∞. This is elegant and gives the method interpretable knobs.

Strong empirical scope: 13 downstream tasks (node- and graph-level) across three real cancer types (breast, lung, colorectal) using TCGA and LINCS data, with consistent (if sometimes modest) improvements over five strong baselines including SOTA augmentation-free SGRL.

Extensive and genuinely useful appendix experiments that substantially strengthen the paper: ablation on the τ_a temperature validating Corollary 1 empirically, embedding-dimension sweep, statistical significance testing, comparisons against augmentation-adjustment/augmentation-free methods (GCA, AFGRL, SimGRACE), link-prediction evaluation, cross-domain/cross-cancer robustness analysis, robustness to GRN estimation noise and reduced sample sizes, and biological enrichment (GO/KEGG) analysis of learned embeddings showing biologically meaningful clustering (e.g., separation of autophagy regulation vs. execution, endocrine resistance pathways).

Practical grounding in real, large-scale public datasets (TCGA, LINCS) with careful, well-documented preprocessing (Bayesian network structure learning via B-spline regression), improving reproducibility.
Honest and specific discussion of limitations (cross-cancer-type generalization failure at fine-tuning), rather than vague hedging.
weaknesses: Reported gains over the strongest baselines are often small, and the paper's own significance testing (Appendix F.4) shows that most SupGCL-vs-baseline differences are not statistically significant after Bonferroni correction; only a handful of comparisons (mostly against weaker baselines like GraphCL and SGRL on select node tasks) reach significance. This somewhat undercuts the abstract's claim of "consistently outperforms" in a statistically meaningful sense.

Cross-domain/OOD generalization is notably poor (Table 18): a model fine-tuned on one cancer type applied directly to another shows substantial performance drops (e.g., BP accuracy falling from 0.282 to 0.163), which limits the practical generality of the pretrained representations despite the paper's motivation of building broadly useful GRN embeddings.

The method's applicability is inherently constrained by the availability of large-scale knockdown/perturbation databases (e.g., LINCS) for the organism/cell types of interest; such supervision may not exist for less-studied diseases or species, limiting generalizability of the approach beyond well-resourced cancer domains.

The biological modeling of a "knockdown augmentation" (zeroing node/edge features) is a simplification; real knockdown effects propagate nonlinearly through the network, and while the teacher GRN is separately re-estimated in this study to capture this, the paper does not fully discuss the mismatch/approximation this creates between the artificial augmentation and the teacher supervision it is compared against.

SupGCL incurs substantially higher pretraining computational cost than baselines (e.g., ~21 hours vs. ~3-11 hours for other methods on breast cancer), which is a nontrivial cost-benefit tradeoff given the often marginal accuracy gains.

Evaluation is limited to three cancer types and a single GNN backbone (Graph Transformer); while some encoder-choice justification is given in the appendix, broader architecture or disease-domain diversity would strengthen claims of general applicability.
